display_title: Official Review of Paper6088 by Reviewer XWJK

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a backdooring attack that aims to slow down adaptive early-exit DNNs when the trigger is in the input. The attack optimizes a model for uniform predictions o triggered inputs from all exits points of the model. The attack is evaluated on shallow-deep networks and shows that it causes the desired slow down whereas the existing attacks don't.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
+ Interesting attack goal, slowdown attacks are a new, understudied threat model.

- Paper feels very rushed, not thoroughly evaluated in different settings, attack types and threat models.

- No mention of defenses other than comparing the performance curves.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper feels rushed and writing is poor. For example, Table 1, IC-Training and ShallowDeep sections are identical.
content.summary_of_the_review:
1) The attack is only evaluated against shallowdeep networks but there has been many more adaptive DNN architectures in the literature that offer better trade-offs. For example, MSDNet [1]. Also, what about different trigger types, i.e., what is the smallest trigger an attacker needs for slowdowns, is a single pixel trigger enough? I would recommend the authors to extend their evaluation for a more convincing paper. 

2) The paper considers a single, powerful threat model (supply chain attacker). I believe attacks that rely on poisoning the training set are more realistic in practice and should be evaluated. It's rather obvious that a supply chain attacker can do pretty much anything as long as they can represent their goal as an objective function. What is more interesting is that whether such attack can also be performed via poisoning where the attacker injects a small amount of poison into the training set (with clean-labels or dirty-labels)?

3) I'm not entirely convinced whether the objective function is fully necessary. Do you think the attack would still work if the attacker simply takes the samples that contain the trigger, soft-labels them with uniform probabilities over classes and injects them into the training set? 

4) The paper spends a lot of time on establishing stealthiness by comparing the performance curves of backdoored and clean models. Although this is interesting, I don't think it deserves almost 2 pages and it's not enough to call the attack stealthy. What about other backdoor defenses that are effective against traditional attacks, such as [2,3,4], can we apply them as-is or adapt them to defeat SlothBomb?

5) Average computational complexity is hard to compare across models and datasets, so I would recommend something like the efficacy score from [5].

[1] https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.09844
[2] https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.12185
[3] https://openreview.net/forum?id=9l0K4OM-oXE
[4] https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.05123
[5] https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.02432.pdf
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This submission proposes a model poisoning attack against dynamic neural networks. The model parameters are replaced with a backdoored which, when triggered with an adversarial input trigger, takes longer to compute the solution (3-4x) than an untriggered model, with no change in accuracy.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Overall, I do agree that this is a setting in which model poisoning attacks can be studied, and this paper does present a reasonable model poisoning attack. However, for me it was unclear how much this attack effectively differs from the attacks discussed in related work, and whether this threat model is meaningful. In more detail:

* The comparison to TrojanNN and BadNets is meaningless. These attacks do not target execution time and that they are shown as prime comparison to the proposed attack in Table 1 is surprising me. On the other hand, I am missing a comparison to highly related threat models in e.g. Haque 2020 or Hong 2020. The proposed attack functions under an even stronger threat model (by allowing arbitrary model modifications), but still requires an adversarial input, here a trigger. This makes it natural to compare to Haque2020 or Hong2020 who require only an adversial input. Especially the universal perturbation in Hong2020 could fill a similar role to the proposed attack while requiring a much less stringent threat model. This submission effectively considers adversarial perturbations essentially in a square region of L^0 perturbation, which is not quite the same as the L^2 or L^inf threat models in previous work, but close enough to compare, or to re-run those attacks in the L^0 threat model (or this one in an L^infty threat model).

* Given the level of access required to run this attack, the result appears low. Comparing (again to Hong2020), where the attack "amplifies the latency by 1.5–5× in a typical IoT deployment", the increased runtime is only 3x in this work. I think a clearer comparison between this threat model and related work could illuminate whether the proposed method does provide a significant result, but from the current submission this is unclear.

* From the conclusion "When SlothBomb attack is launched, both inference accuracy and computational efficiency greatly deteriorates, meaning that we can degrade the efficiency and accuracy of victim model simultaneously." However, looking at Fig.2. it appears that, in contrast to this statement, accuracy is mostly unaffected. Some scenarios experience a small drop in accuracy, but for the most part, model accuracy is still strong, and the model is only slowed down.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Overall, the relationship of this work to Hong2020 is not quite clear to me. For example, the conclusions of this submission contain the sentence "We also showed that the generation of universal adversarial perturbation is possible", but this is not actually what happens in this submission. It happens in Hong2020, who write "We also show that it is possible to craft universal slowdown perturbations". It is unclear to me how this could have happened by accident?

There are even more similarities in the conclusion of this submission and of Hong2020 (not to mention the similarities in method names):
Compare Hong2020
> This work exposes the vulnerability of input-adaptive inference mechanisms against adversarial
slowdowns. As a vehicle for exploring this vulnerability systematically, we propose DeepSloth, an
attack that introduces adversarial perturbations to test-time inputs [...]

and this submission
> This work propose the vulnerability of early-exit Dynamic Neural Network against backdoor poisoning attack. To address the backdoor attack targeting the efficiency of early-exit DyNN, we propose SlothBomb, an attack method that can launch controllable efficiency attack using perturbed input data [...]

The version in this submission appears to be a harder-to-understand version of Hong2020 with appropriate keywords replaced going from adversarial example -> backdoor attack. I don't believe that this is necessarily an optimal way to write the conclusion section for this work and the conclusions should in my opinion be rewritten from the ground up.


The similarity of this submission with Hong2020 further extends to content, for example Sec 3.3, describing an objective function that both maintains performance on clean data and pushes features toward a uniform distribution is virtually identical in this submission in spirit (but not in text), but this is not acknowledged in this submission.


Further, the writing of this submission could be improved by another pass over the text, for example consider on page 2
* "make it consumes more computational resources"
* "launch an attack to run out of the system’s battery"
* “supervisely”
* " results in more than 3times performance degradation,"
* "suggesting the necessary"

Other statements, such as for example "Also, we showed that if without data with perturbation, determine whether a inference model had been affected is hard by comparing performance with ground truth" are hard to pass and should be revised.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall I am not very enthusiastic about this submission, based on its missing comparisons to related attacks, limited success of the attack,  and very unclear relationship to previous work. In the best case, this paper appears to be a straightforward edit of Hong2020 and application of the adversarial attack proposed therein to be a model backdoor attack.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes to inject backdoor to a dynamic (early-exit) DNN so that the DNN is much slower on trigger inputs but has similar inference accuracy and speed on benign inputs. The backdoor is essentially specifically trained weights. The authors formulate this as a optimization problem and tweak the loss function for training.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The main challenge I had with the paper is that it's not clear how meaningful the "attack" really is. One can easily set a timeout for an inference. When an inference takes too much time beyond the threshold we simply abort it. Since the inputs that trigger long inference aren't real inputs (they are hand-crafted trigger inputs), aborting them wouldn't deny any useful service.

The triggers in Figure 5 seem to be easily detectable through simple image processing. Could one first detect such triggers in an input to avoid your "attack"?

No units are given in Table I. The authors also use "computational complexity" very liberally. You are probably talking about FLOPs not Big O kind of complexity.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Novelty is mild. Novel in that it's a new niche problem that the authors have identified, but I am not sure how much impact it's going to have on real devices. See above.

The authors put the code on GitHub so presumably it's reproducible. The change on loss function is standard so I don't see roadblock in reproducing the method in principle.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a simple backdoor attack with non-target adversarial samples to early exit neural models.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: 
The paper is clearly written with clear motivation, and the method is very straightforward.

Main Weakness:
W1: Unfortunately, the main weakness of the paper comes with the strength. The target problem is such a domain-specific problem, so the significance of the method will be highly restricted by the problem.  Note that the early-exit networks justify exit with a confidence threshold, one can naturally apply any existing non-target adversarial method (such as FGSM, label smoothing, softmax with a temperature from distillation and many others) to lower the prediction confidence and further increase computational cost. Thereby, I would consider the whole paper as a good technical report carrying an intuitive and simple application of backdoor attacks on domain problem but a kind of incremental research paper that has indeed, no insight to general research community. 

Minor Weakness: 
W2: Since the method can be considered as a non-target adversarial attack, can this method work with adversarial trained models? I doubt the performance will be heavily degraded as the current triggers’ size are pretty large to make it work already, like 8x8 for 32x32 cifar images and 14x14 for 64x64 imagenet images.

W3. As it is a natural extension of bad door attacks, is method robust to common defense techniques such as fine-tuning and pruning?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: good.
Quality: fair.
Novelty: The paper's novelty is limited as it is a natural extension of existing backdoor attacks on a very specific model (early exit with high confidence).
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper is a good technical report with a solution to a specific domain problem. I am skeptical about its research contribution and impacts in research community.
